svg.aria-label: Diagram: application objects and service principals in Microsoft Entra ID, showing the single application object in the home tenant against one service principal per tenant where the application is used, the three types of service principal, the asymmetry where deleting an application object also deletes its home tenant service principal but restoring it does not restore the service principal, and the consent-driven flow that creates a service principal in each consuming tenant
svg.title: One application, two objects — and the copy in your tenant is the one that decides what it can do
svg.text: One application. Two objects. Two portal pages. Endless confusion.
The blueprint lives in one tenant and may not be yours. The instance lives in every tenant that uses it, and governs what it can do there.
Application object — the blueprint
“A Microsoft Entra application is defined by its one and
only application object”, in the tenant where it was
registered — the application’s “home” tenant.
“Used as a template or blueprint”. The docs compare it
to “a class in object-oriented programming”.
Portal: App registrations
One-to-one with the software application.
Service principal — the instance
“A service principal is created in every tenant where the
application is used.”
It “defines what the app can actually do in the specific
tenant, who can access the app, and what resources
the app can access.”
Portal: Enterprise applications
One-to-many from the application object.
Three kinds of service principal, and only one has an application object behind it
Application
the local instance of a global application object. The ordinary case.
Managed identity
“can be granted access and permissions, but can’t be updated or modified
directly”, and “doesn’t have an associated app object” — posts #35, #36
Legacy
no app registration behind it, and “can only be used in the tenant where
it was created”
What propagates, what does not, and what does not come back
Delete cascades. Restore does not.
“Deleting an application object will also delete its home
tenant service principal object.”
“However, restoring that application object through the
app registrations UI won’t restore its corresponding
service principal.”
Undo gets you the blueprint back and not the identity
that held the role assignments. Deactivate instead.
Edits stop at the home tenant
“Any changes that you make to your application object
are also reflected in its service principal object in the
application’s home tenant only.”
So a multitenant app that adds a permission does not
acquire it in tenants that already consented.
And via Microsoft Graph, “creating the service principal
object is a separate step” — the portal does both.
How a service principal arrives in a tenant that does not own the application
Adatum
home tenant · app object
consent
Contoso
its own service principal
Fabrikam
its own service principal
Each consumer tenant keeps control
“over what the application is allowed to
do via the corresponding service
principal object in each tenant.”
A single-tenant application has only one service principal, in its home tenant. A multitenant application gains one in every tenant that consents.
And they stop at the cloud boundary: multitenant applications “don’t function across cloud boundaries due to the segregation of service
principal authorities within each cloud” — the authority URLs differ, .com against .us, and the process fails (post #6).
Sources: Apps and service principals in Microsoft Entra ID, and Application model, on Microsoft Learn.
